tagline.text: Meeting the Philippines' "grandfather mountain" above the clouds

location.label: Location
location.text: Digos & Santa Cruz, Davao del Sur; Kidapawan, Cotabato

Jay Jopia / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: At about

, the Philippines' highest mountain. Passing through mossy forest, the alpine Lake Venado, and a vast rocky slope wreathed in sulfur smoke, you reach the summit to a sea of clouds spread over Mindanao — a mountain indigenous communities revere as sacred, calling it their "grandfather."
Mount Apo stands about

tall, the highest mountain in the Philippines. A massive stratovolcano spanning Davao City, Davao del Sur, and Cotabato province, it has no recorded historical eruption, yet it remains a potentially active volcano, still venting sulfur gas near the summit today. "Apo" means grandfather or elder in several Philippine languages, and for the Bagobo, Manobo, and other indigenous groups living on its slopes, it's a sacred mountain where ancestral spirits are believed to dwell. They also call it "Sandawa."
Mount Apo was designated a national park in

and is now protected as Mount Apo Natural Park, also listed as an ASEAN Heritage Park. Its slopes rise from lowland rainforest into thick, moss-draped cloud forest, then into stunted shrubland, home to hundreds of bird species — including the endangered Philippine eagle — and rare plants. Lake Venado, at about
, is one of the highest lakes in the Philippines, and most climbers camp here.
Climbing Mount Apo is a bucket-list challenge for any Filipino hiker. It requires no technical rock climbing, but you'll need to climb and descend steep dirt trails, tree roots, and rocky slopes for
8–10 hours

a day, and near the summit, night temperatures can drop to around 5 degrees, so both stamina and preparation matter. The "Boulder Face" on the Santa Cruz route in particular is a slope of massive stacked boulders, with sulfur smoke rising from cracks between them — a scene that feels like another planet.

Compared with other popular Philippine mountains, the climbing rules here are stricter: a permit and a registered local guide are required. It's recommended for anyone with hiking experience and the stamina for a 2–3 day camping trek, or those who want to see a sea of clouds and sunrise from the Philippines' highest summit. First-time hikers should build experience on an easier mountain, like Pinatubo or Pulag in Luzon, before attempting this one.

blocks.title: Sunrise and sea of clouds at the summit

children.text: Leaving camp at

and reaching the summit reveals a sea of clouds spreading below, and on a clear day, Davao Gulf and the Cotabato plains far beyond. A photo at the marker for the Philippines' highest point is the highlight of this climb.
Camp beside a lake and meadow spread across a highland plateau at about
. Mist settles over the lake at dusk, and at night the sky fills with stars.

A section on the Santa Cruz route where you scramble over a slope of massive boulders, with smoke and yellow sulfur crystals from fumaroles creating an otherworldly scene. It's the hardest stretch, but also the most memorable.
Above about
, cloud forest appears, with tree trunks and rocks thickly covered in moss. The mist drifting through the forest gives it a fairy-tale atmosphere.
Near the summit are several peaks and traces of an old crater. With your guide, you can explore the highest peak and the crater rim, observing the volcanic terrain.

At the trailhead, there may be rituals or guidance from the indigenous community, and most local guides and porters come from communities on the mountain's slopes. Listening to their stories and learning how to approach the mountain is part of the Mount Apo climbing experience.
After descending, confirming your successful climb at the registration office earns you a climbing certificate — a treasured memento for Filipino hikers.

Register, receive a safety briefing, get assigned a guide and porter, and start the climb.

Explore the peaks and crater around the summit and take photos.
If traversing, head toward Santa Cruz across Boulder Face to the descent camp; if it's an out-and-back climb, return to the Lake Venado camp to rest.
Descend the remaining stretch to your starting point or the registration office on the other side.
Confirm your completed climb, receive your certificate, and head back to Davao to rest.
A direct flight from Manila to Davao Airport (DVO) takes about
1 hour 50 minutes
, and about
1 hour 10 minutes
from Cebu. For the Kidapawan route on the Cotabato side, it's about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
from Davao Airport by car. It's best to arrive in Davao the day before your climb and rest for a day.
For the Kapatagan route, take a bus or van from the Davao Ecoland terminal (DCOTT) to Digos, about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
(about
), then transfer to a jeepney or habal-habal bound for Kapatagan, another
1 hour
in. For the Santa Cruz route, take a Santa Cruz-bound bus from downtown Davao, about
1 hour
, then continue by vehicle to the trailhead. The Kidapawan route is about
2–3 hours
from Davao by Cotabato-bound bus.
Since Mount Apo requires a permit and guide, and transport to the trailhead is inconvenient, most climbers use a registered local tour operator or mountaineering club package. A
2 nights, 3 days
package runs about

per person, usually including permit fees, entrance fees, guide fees, meals, and round-trip transport from Davao. Porter fees and personal gear rental are often separate, so check the included items carefully.
Mount Apo is out of the typhoon path, but as a mountainous area it sees frequent rain year-round. The best time is the comparatively dry
February
to
May
, and
March–April
especially has more clear days for good summit views. From
June
to
November
, afternoon rain and fog are frequent, turning the trail muddy and often blocking the summit view, and December–
January
also sees plenty of rain.

Near the summit and Lake Venado, daytime temperatures run 10–15 degrees and can drop to around 5 degrees at dawn, with wind making it feel even colder. Mount Apo Natural Park's management committee sets an annual rest period to let the ecosystem recover and limits the number of daily climbers. In
, a major wildfire closed the mountain for a long time. Applications fill up quickly around Holy Week and holidays, so book at least 2–4 weeks ahead.
The rest period runs for three months every year,
June 1–August 31
, during which climbing and camping are banned on all trails on the Davao and Cotabato sides, and it was enforced the same way in
. In years of severe drought, the mountain is temporarily closed even in the dry season because of wildfire risk, and in
March–April 2024
it was closed for more than a month. Plan your climb between
September and May
, and check the latest announcements from the DENR and each local tourism office before you go.

and may vary depending on local conditions. Permit fees and climbing rules may change under the unified trekking policy, so check the latest updates.

Staying in downtown Davao is most convenient before and after the climb, since most tour operators gather there, and it offers a hot shower and a proper meal after descending. Business hotels downtown run about
a night. If you'd rather stay a night near the trailhead beforehand, a pension in downtown Digos (about
) or a simple homestay near Kapatagan or Kidapawan is available.

Meals on the mountain are usually included in the tour package, centered on rice, canned goods, instant noodles, and simple side dishes. For trail snacks, pack plenty of chocolate, nuts, dried mango, and energy bars. After descending, enjoying a hearty meal like grilled tuna jaw or bulalo in Davao is a favorite way for hikers to recover. Descending via Kidapawan brings you near hot springs and fruit farms, where you can try seasonal durian or marang.
Permit applications often require a copy of your ID and a medical certificate confirming you're fit to climb. It's best to get this from a clinic 1–2 weeks before departure.
Keep your personal load light and hire a porter — it makes a big difference to your energy management. One porter typically carries around 15 kg.
Waterproof hiking boots, a waterproof jacket, insulating fleece or a light down jacket, gloves, and a beanie are essential. It's hot by day and very cold at night, so layering matters.
Bring a headlamp with spare batteries, trekking poles, and a water bottle that holds at least 2 liters. Water around camp must always be filtered or boiled before drinking.
Phone signal drops out almost entirely on the mountain. Let your family know your itinerary and your tour operator's contact details before you leave.
To catch sunrise at the summit, you need to set out around
3 a.m.
. It helps to go to bed early the evening before and keep trail snacks in your pocket.
All trash must be carried back out, and some trailheads inspect for trash on the way down.
Holy Week and holidays see a rush of applications with limited slots, so if you have a specific date in mind, start looking into reservations a month ahead.
Climbing without a permit or entering the mountain without a registered guide is prohibited. If caught, your climb may be halted and you may face a fine.
Hypothermia is a risk near the summit. Change out of rain-soaked clothes right away, and never leave your insulating layers behind.
Near the sulfur fumaroles on Boulder Face, move through quickly to avoid inhaling the gas for long, and tell your guide in advance if you have a respiratory condition.
Dirt trails and rocks get very slippery when it rains. Don't push your pace, and follow your guide if they decide to turn back.
Mount Apo is sacred to indigenous communities. Avoid loud noise at the summit or taking rocks and plants, and respect the community's rules.
Because of wildfire risk, campfires and smoking at camp are strictly banned or restricted.
Mount Apo strictly enforces a "no permit, no climb" policy. Be sure to secure a permit and guide through a certified operator or the park office before setting out.
